title: Time-spectral control of accidental coincidences in daylight entanglement-based free-space QKD
authors: Jiyoung Moon, Yonggi Jo, Zaeill Kim, Yong Sup Ihn, Nam Hun Park
abstract: Daylight entanglement-based free-space quantum key distribution (QKD) is limited by accidental coincidences from receiver-admitted background light. We develop and experimentally validate a receiver-level framework linking receiver bandwidth, accepted temporal width, and background-noise density to Bob singles, sifted-key rate, error rate, and quantum bit error rate (QBER) in telecom-wavelength BBM92 QKD. Indoor sweeps show that useful sifted counts saturate near the source-matched bandwidth, whereas broader bandwidth or higher background mainly increases accidental contamination. Increasing the accepted temporal width leaves Bob singles nearly unchanged but directly raises QBER by enlarging the random-overlap probability. A two-dimensional design map shows that the temporal-window margin contracts rapidly with increasing background-to-signal ratio, while the bandwidth margin remains comparatively broad near source-matched filtering. A 10 m rooftop daylight experiment demonstrates operation in the predicted low-accidental regime, yielding a mean sifted-key rate of 2,811 cps and a mean QBER of 4.43%.
summary: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for controlling accidental coincidences in free-space QKD links operating under daylight conditions. By modeling the impact of receiver bandwidth and temporal acceptance windows, the authors quantify how background noise degrades key rates and increases errors. The work validates this theory with both controlled indoor sweeps and a successful 10 m outdoor demonstration.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is mitigating performance degradation in free-space Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) due to accidental coincidences caused by background daylight illumination.
main_result: The authors developed a quantitative framework demonstrating that the sifted key rate and QBER can be controlled by optimizing receiver spectral bandwidth and accepted temporal window, achieving high rates in outdoor daylight conditions.
method: They employ a rate-equation model to decompose the coincidence count into true signal, source-originated accidentals, and background-induced accidentals, validating this against systematic indoor sweeps and an outdoor rooftop test.
model_or_system: The system is based on telecom-wavelength BBM92 QKD using entangled photon pairs in a free-space link. The model incorporates detector dead-time effects, spectral filtering (bandwidth $\Delta\lambda$), and temporal acceptance windows ($T_{	ext{win}}$) to quantify the accidental coincidence budget.
key_observables: Sifted-key rate ($\approx 2,811 	ext{ cps}$), Quantum Bit Error Rate ($	ext{QBER} \approx 4.43\%$), and the accidental coincidence fraction ($f_{	ext{acc}}$).
important_parameters: Background-to-signal ratio ($ho = N_0/S_0$); receiver bandwidth ($\Delta\lambda$); accepted temporal width ($T_{	ext{win}}$).
main_assumptions: The framework uses non-paralyzable dead-time corrections and treats multi-click rejection via estimated survival probabilities; the model is designed for rate estimation rather than full microscopic hardware simulation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate indoor testbed setups, spectral/temporal characterizations (histograms), 2D design maps showing how $f_{	ext{acc}}$ and QBER vary with bandwidth and temporal window margin under varying background ratios, and final performance metrics from the 10 m rooftop experiment.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical limitations of daylight free-space QKD due to background light. It then develops a comprehensive rate-level model linking receiver filtering parameters ($\Delta\lambda$, $T_{	ext{win}}$) to key performance metrics (sifted rate, QBER). The methodology is validated through detailed indoor sweeps before concluding with successful operation demonstration over a 10 m outdoor link.
why_interesting: This work provides critical engineering insights into the practical limitations of quantum communication in real-world environments by rigorously modeling noise sources. For theorists working on open quantum systems, it offers an excellent case study in characterizing environmental coupling (background light) and designing optimal filtering strategies to maintain coherence/fidelity.
